native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.lineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.asExprString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    balanced():String = self

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.stringEquals")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.charAt")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareTo")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareToIgnoreCase")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaSubstr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.indexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenate")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenateChar")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do
        if self.isEmpty then b
        elif b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
        else
            typecase b.asFlatString of
                f:FlatString ⇒ flatConcat(self, f)
                f:String ⇒ concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
            end
        end
    end

    opr ||(self, b:Char): String =
        if |self| ≥ maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b.asString)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end

    splitWithOffsets():ZeroIndexed⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧ = Nothing⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧
    split():Generator⟦String⟧ = Nothing⟦String⟧

    writeOn(stream: WriteStream): () = stream.write(self)

end FlatString

end

content.content:
# Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## After the landing: the coordinator's routing

The coordinator's steps after a landing, in this order, each done whole:

1. The landing report to the curator.
2. The routing: every open row, record default and item for the curator filed with a batch or as a parked line of `PLAN.md`. Each is checked against POSITIONS and the notes `INDEX.md` lists before it is called open, put to the curator or briefed. In the same pass the routing moves out of `PLAN.md` each item the batch built or answered, and any item it finds stale: word for word, into `PLAN-history.md`, under the landing's dated heading and the heading the item stood under. The batch's own line in its phase becomes one line, with its landing commit and its review. An open item whose text also stands in another home (a `review-queue.md` entry, a ledger row, a FACTS or POSITIONS entry) becomes one line in `PLAN.md`: what is asked, its default, and a pointer to that home. No other step takes an item out of `PLAN.md`, which held 519K characters before its consolidation of 2026-10-15, 54 % of them closed (`process-engineering/plan-map.md`, sections 2 and 4).
3. FACTS consolidated as its README says, superseded text moved to `FACTS-history.md`. The commit stage has already written the landed count and distance, and the two stages' seconds (F-53, F-240).
4. The skills, in three moves:
   - One task for the standing skill writer (`tools/skill-writer.sh`, its brief `skill-writer-brief.md`): the batch's revival-change material, the section "Revival changes, for the skill writer" of its `RECORD.md`; the skill sentences that the post-batch review lists as false; and any `skill-touched` item. The writer runs `tools/skills-lint.py` before each commit.
   - A cold read of the parts the writer changed, by an agent given only the skill and `skill-cold-read-brief.md`.
   - The writer fixes the cold read's flags, and the coordinator pushes its commits.
5. The next batch launched only after that, so that its workers read the updated skill (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The landing").
6. The combined post-batch review, started at the landing, since step 4 takes its list of false skill sentences (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The landing").

The review explains every new or risen row of the checker count by a named rung edit. It reads the microGPT walk check's result. It reports the batch's measures against the batches before it with `tools/batch-measures.py` on the run's directory (`batch-redesign.md`, "The measures").

- F-44 **The compiled checker enforces the multiple instantiation exclusion rule and relies on it, and the one library meets the rule.** The rule: no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait. The checker's Return Type Rule relies on it: with the rule relaxed alone, a program passes the checker and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` (`OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`; the probe `ProbeMIEPick`). The team's JVM type mapping relies on it too: no closure of extends lists names one generic at two static arguments, so the class that template expansion makes for an instantiation carries the type relations over as Java ones (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:125`, read). F-48 gives the kinds of static argument that the rule compares. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion: it accepts a type that extends two instantiations, and its overloading check does not count them as excluding (row 416; the review's section 3). P-43 keeps the rule. Besides the flat number tower of P-43, the library meets it by three changes of `952892a00`: `TotalComparison` extends `Comparison` and `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, no longer `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]`; `AnyMaybe` extends `AnyUniqueItem` alone, no longer `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` beside it; and `andCondCombine` chooses `andRelCond` by a `typecase`, in place of a second `ANDCOND`. So under walk, a program's `p1 ANDCOND p2` of two relational predicates, conditions built from a relation over a generator, which `filter` fuses, is no longer itself a relational predicate (row 458). - F-172 **The specification's integer chapter states the library's integer rules.** `narrow` converts a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` to `ZZ32`, and an `NN64` to `NN32`, by keeping the low 32 bits; a value that does not fit wraps, and nothing is thrown. `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` work on the five integer types. On `ZZ` they are `shift`, which is exact at any count. On a fixed-size type, `LSHIFT` loses the bits shifted out and throws nothing. `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, and one that a fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`. At a negative power, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 throws `DivisionByZero`, and any other base throws `IntegerOverflow`. The library follows the same power rule under walk; the compiled path's own library does not (F-263). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-62` (`narrow` and the shifts) and `:530-542` (the power); `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-268` (`GCD` and `LCM`).
--- NEW F-172

Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-98` (the conversions and the shifts) and `:562-574` (the power); `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-268` (`GCD` and `LCM`).
An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

Among the explicit conversions, each of the five integer types has the getters
\VAR{asZZ32}, \VAR{asZZ64}, \VAR{asNN32}, \VAR{asNN64} and \VAR{asZZ}, which
convert a value to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and keep the value: where the type
converted to does not hold the value, \TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
The getter to a value's own type returns the value, and a getter to a type that
coerces from the value's type gives the value of the coercion.
Each fixed-size type also has a getter that keeps the bits of a value and reads
them at the same width with the other sign: \VAR{bitsAsNN32} of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \VAR{bitsAsNN64} of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{bitsAsZZ32} of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and \VAR{bitsAsZZ64} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}.

The methods \VAR{narrow}, \VAR{widen}, \VAR{signed}, \VAR{unsigned} and
\VAR{big} also convert, and throw no \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
The method \VAR{narrow} converts a value of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} to
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a value of \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, by
keeping its low 32 bits: the result is the value of the narrower type that is
congruent to the argument modulo \EXP{2^{32}}.
A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other wraps.
The method \VAR{widen} converts a value of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} to
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and a value of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and
\VAR{big} a value of any integer type to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, each keeping the value.
The method \VAR{unsigned} converts a value of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} to
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and a value of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and
\VAR{signed} converts the other way, each keeping the bits as the getters
\VAR{bitsAsNN32}, \VAR{bitsAsNN64}, \VAR{bitsAsZZ32} and \VAR{bitsAsZZ64} do.
Each of the five methods is declared on every integer type to which it applies,
and returns a value of its result type unchanged: \VAR{narrow} of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, \VAR{widen} of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
and of \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \VAR{signed} of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{unsigned} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and \VAR{big} of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}.
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} has neither \VAR{narrow} nor \VAR{widen}: a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} converts to a fixed-size type only by a getter.
\revision{revival-int-conversions}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named
none of these conversions, which \library\ declare on the integer types; the
two paragraphs above state the getters and the methods the revival decided for
them, and \VAR{narrow} no longer converts a value of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}.}

The operators \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT} shift the bits of an integer of any of
the five types by a count of any integer type, and return a value of the type of
the integer shifted.
On \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,k)} and
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,-k)}.
On a fixed-size type of width \VAR{n}, for a nonnegative count \VAR{k},
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\lfloor x/2^{k} \rfloor}, and
\EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is the value of the type that is congruent to
\EXP{x \cdot 2^{k}} modulo \EXP{2^{n}}: the bits shifted out are lost, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
So a count at or beyond the width gives \EXP{0} for a left shift, and for a right
shift \EXP{0}, or \EXP{-1} if \VAR{x} is negative.
A negative count shifts the other way: \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} (-k)} is
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k}, and \EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} (-k)} is \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k}.
The count is read by its value, whatever its type: an \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} count of
\EXP{2^{63}} or more is beyond the width, not negative.
\revision{revival-shifts}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named neither
\VAR{narrow} nor \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT}, which \library\ declare on the
integer types; the paragraph above states the rules the revival decided for the
shifts, and the paragraph on the methods that keep bits, before it, the rule for
\VAR{narrow} (\secref{revival-int-conversions}).}

- F-333 **The one library's arrays hold their elements in a Java-backed store in a field, which walk answers with its own `AtomicArray`.** `NativeArray` is a plain component. `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` hold a `JavaArrayStore` of `FortressLibrary` in the field `mem` and read it through `cast[\T\]`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array` holds a `JavaRR64ArrayStore`, and is in the api, but no factory chooses it (P-84, P-85). The stores' 7 bindings name `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over two compiled classes: `FortressArrayStore`, an `Object[]` whose elements the compiled transaction keys by array and index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`), and `FortressRR64ArrayStore`, a `double[]`. NamingCzar's walk-world table reads the two classes as the two traits. Walk's loader answers each `arrayOps` name with `ArrayOps$<name>` over `FortressBuiltin`'s private `JavaArrayStoreObject`, an `AtomicArray`, or `JavaRR64ArrayStoreObject`, a `double[]`; it refuses at load a name with no operation. A second initialisation is ignored in both arrays, by walk's store and by `FortressArrayStore` (row 466); the two RR64 stores write it and answer `true`, as `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s glue did. F-299 counts the bindings. Tests: `tests/ArrayStoreWalk`, `ArrayStoreRR64Walk`, `ArrayInitOnceWalk`, `ArrayOpsMisspeltWalk`, `compiler/runtimeValues/ArrayStoreJUTest`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-array-store/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
11:**5. Walk's immutable arrays: one rule for a second initialisation (rung A; fork A7; row 466).** A7 reads "the store keeps today's rule that a second initialisation of an element is ignored". That was the mutable array's rule. The base's immutable glue overwrote (`interpreter/glue/prim/PrimImmutableArray.java:73-82` at the base). With one store for both, `immutableArray[\ZZ32\](2).fill(3).fill(4)` now holds `3 3`, not `4 4` (`tests/ArrayInitOnceWalk.fss`). The two RR64 stores still write a second initialisation and answer `true` (`FortressRR64ArrayStore.java:24-27`; `ArrayOps.java:68-73`; skeptic A's correction 3), as `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s glue did. So row 466's claim, "the compiled store's `init` keeps the first value as well", holds for the `Object[]` store only. A.worker.2 and A.skeptic.5, `PLAN.md:696`. Default: as landed.

content.content:
- F-132 **Under `walk`, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when the result does not fit, as the specification says.** It builds P-73. Every arithmetic operation on a fixed width whose result can leave its type raises it, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included, and a program can catch it. Three kinds of operation raise nothing: the wrapping operators (F-130) and the low-bits conversions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big`, which keep the bits (P-72; the checked `as…` getters raise, F-331); and the shifts `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT`, which lose the bits shifted out (F-125). Gated by `tests/FixedWidthOverflowRungB.fss` (`+`, `-`, `DOT` (`·`), `DIV`, negation and absolute value, on the four fixed widths) and `tests/PowChooseLcmRungE.fss` (`^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM`). The compiled path is outside this fact. Its known gaps: the compiler prelude's ranges raise `IntegerOverflow` where their bounds sum beyond `ZZ32` (row 453); and `^` saturates, throws an uncatchable Java exception or adds (rows 523 to 525). Its `CHOOSE` raises `IntegerOverflow` as walk's does (F-305). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overflow-natives/REPORT.md` section 13; `compile-ladder/rung-size-range/REPORT.md` section 12.
- P-72 **`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a value that the narrower type cannot hold, signed and unsigned, on both paths, and raises no `IntegerOverflow`.** The decision covers `narrow` from a `ZZ64` to a `ZZ32` and from an `NN64` to an `NN32`. A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other becomes the value of the narrower type with the same low 32 bits. Why: the team's specification said nothing on `narrow`, and the team's boundary test `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss` asserts the low 32 bits for `NN64` values. On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits is a bit operation, like a shift, and the signed `narrow` gets the same answer.
